Soleil Saint-Cyr

Soleil Saint-Cyr

Depleted Shells

contra Coumba Samba’s Stars and Stripes

In Coumba Samba’s visual art, familiar objects and bright colors create a Lynchian experience of domesticity; malicious forces lurk beneath her shiny surfaces. With “Stars and Stripes,” Samba presents her first solo exhibition in the United States and becomes, at only 26, one of the Whitney Museum of American Art’s youngest-ever solo exhibitors. Her previous projects often feature found objects which encapsulate the global supply chain’s exploitation of African countries; the mundane in her installations straddles the gap between everyday existence and international politics, often amassing depth as unplumbable as the supply chain itself in doing so. Her primary pursuit as a visual artist is most effective when it simultaneously holds the intimate and international realms in perspective to highlight the individual’s role in complex systems of modernity. “Stars and Stripes” attempts a similar maneuver for the issue of nuclear development, but Samba loses sight of the very individuals she seeks to educate and implicate.

I enjoy considering each of Samba’s engagements with the arts — music, fashion, visual — as a part of a greater philosophy in “herself-as-readymade.” She moonlights as a singer in the cheekily-named electronic duo (and recent ear opener) New York and as a model for luxury fashion houses like Balenciaga. But while shooting editorials or making trendy glitchpop, she does not simply mannequin luxury clothing or set the language of the Internet to song; she embodies the strange encounters caused by globalization. Although she has lived and worked in Europe since her undergraduate studies, New York is the city of her birth and part-time residence, and her dual identity as both a Senegalese-American resident of the US and UK and an artist interested in history’s present manifestations exposes the economics which make possible that clothing’s and music’s existence.

Rufus Knuppel

Rufus Knuppel

Coxon Day

“This messianic moment...has created a tribal frenzy in the Bay that will soon spill its bounds.”

It just so happened that the day everything changed, the day AI safety went mainstream, I was sitting in a multi-story fortress of autists and cracked researchers in Berkeley, California called Constellation, the center of what can only be termed The Resistance — a place that hums with excitement, and fervor, and a terrific sense that humanity is aboard a fast-moving, many-trillion-dollar locomotive called Artificial Intelligence, that the train is careening toward doom, and that this makeshift AI safety movement, brewing for decades in the dank parts of the internet and now headquartered in the East Bay, is the only thing that can stop it.

That day, September 8th, was the day Jacob Coxon, a 27-year-old ML researcher, resigned from Anthropic, warning: “I spent the last three years doing pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic. Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Anthropic’s Alignment Science lead, Evan Hubinger, then quote-tweeted Coxon: “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade. I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to.” By September 9th, Jacob’s tweet had made every front page and nightly news program in America. The ensuing maelstrom of discourse, in a matter of hours, brought “x-risk” and “p(doom)” from the fringes of American intellectual life to the bull’s-eye of public consciousness. Eliezer Yudkowsky, the portly forefather of the AI safety movement, declared momentary victory on X, the agora of AI: “Happy Coxon Day to all who will one day celebrate it.”

Over the next decade, our political life will undergo a total transformation. The tectonic continents of Left and Right will shudder, fracture, and re-form. Ideas and ideologies, so long fossilized in our institutions, will be liquidated and repoured. The first glimmers of that societal revolution are, right now, appearing all around us. But the battle lines of this new era will be drawn from geography altogether strange and foreign to the electorate: the once obscure, and often extreme, Bay Area factions that have so long labored and lamented over the most significant technological creation of our time.

In the months leading up to Coxon Day, I had a sense that the frontier was accelerating at an unexpectedly ferocious pace, that the mood in the labs was one of apprehension and awe at the capabilities of their own demigod-like creations, and that something — I didn’t know what — was about to collide and explode. And so I wanted to go to SF and witness this happening. My feeling of anticipation was affirmed by a sequence of rumors and releases this summer, from July to early September, each an escalation of the last:

The solution of Navier-Stokes felt like the exclamation point on a cascade of growing capabilities and concern within the AI community. In mathematics, at least, a kind of superintelligence had arrived, though in gruesome, brutish form: a hive of superpersistent agents working together like locusts to raze the great plains where the giants of the discipline — Archimedes, Euler, and Newton — had once grazed. (Now OpenAI has announced the solutions to hundreds more longstanding open problems in mathematics.) The mathematics community, as if besieged by a biblical plague, entered into existential peril. In the words of mathematician Terence Tao, it was the end of “the age of heroes.”

So it was on an unusually hot and radiant day in the Bay — the second day of my trip — that I visited Constellation, the mecca of AI safety, and Jacob Coxon resigned. That morning I had sat in a coffee shop in Oakland, reading the news about Navier-Stokes and feeling very freaked out; things were unfolding just as the labs had promised — it was all going to plan. Models, trained to be good at math and code in the race toward RSI, had first conquered these domains.

I’m not allowed to say what happened inside Constellation — I had to sign something as a member of the media that said I wouldn’t. But besides the grand, turquoise vistas of the Bay, the environs were rather less romantic than what I had imagined the headquarters of the movement that’s saving the world would look like. The Wall Street Journal describes the mundane office space pretty accurately, as a place where AI safety researchers “enjoy catered vegan meals and bring their laptops to couches with sweeping views of the San Francisco Bay. At dinners and happy hours every month, they discuss the latest and scariest AI.” The Constellation people will call that caricature, but caricature is often replete with truth.

Constellation is full of a particular type: the EA, or effective altruist. The thing about EAs is that they’re famously bad at communicating their ideas to the general population and famously good at alienating their allies with their superficial freakishness and incessant need to drive a sympathizer to the precipice of disaffection. A classic confrontation from an EA goes something like: Oh, so you agree that x is bad? Why aren’t you worried about y, then? This is said with sincerity, not antagonism, but with EAs, it’s all aboard the crazy train all the time — and not all of us want to ride that train to its final destination, or even past the first couple stops. So much of what is important about the world of EA and rationalism (I still don’t understand fully how to draw a line between the two) is cloaked in the murkiness of non-normative behavior — polycules, orgies, autistic sexual mores. These prolific taboos create a force field of distrust, or repulsion, around rationalist ideas. EAs are easy to dismiss on the grounds of weirdness, but it is worth one’s while to bushwhack through the unsavory parts to arrive at the core of EA thought: a profound motivation to think cleanly through problems and do what is ultimately (in quantitative terms) most “right.”

I was invited to visit Constellation by a friend named Noah, a UChicago dropout who followed the go-to AI safety pipeline that ferries young, aspiring EAs through internet forums, university clubs (the MIT AI safety club has an operating budget in the millions), and woodsy retreats to Berkeley. Within AI safety, Noah operates like a frat president — he knows everyone, everyone knows him, he’ll key you in with his keycard, he’s very affable, he knows the rules of the space inside and out, and he also has a register for interfacing with outsiders and being an all-around upstanding diplomat for the cause.

Noah will often stop mid-conversation to verbally model a hypothesis in his head; he is charming and steady, and he lives and breathes AI safety, often napping in the office. EA is a kind of religious occupation for many, and Noah (raised a Modern Orthodox Jew) has swapped the Talmud for LessWrong. (My co-editor Elan points out that Noah often reaches for a phantom kippah.) Noah just moved into a group house with some AI safety brethren — housemates are the connective tissue of a great deal of the most important relationships in the Bay. Living together creates a space for trust, alignment, and the rebreathing of ideas.

Safe at SlutCon

“‘You are trying to get a million dollars. The million dollars is stored in his balls.’”

Seduction Camp

Seduction Camp

The two men in our circle were about what I expected. Both were readers of the blog LessWrong and worked for some kind of amorphous tech venture. The other girl and I were “flirt girls,” a compensated worker or volunteer whose job for the weekend was to let men practice flirting on them. The four of us sat cross-legged on a mattress somebody had pulled to the floor. The mattress was so soft that every time the girl next to me shifted her weight, I slid toward her. The people at Lighthaven call this practice “circling”; it asks you to narrate your inner state to others while it happens. If your throat dries when someone looks at you, you announce the dryness to the group.

I was dressed in my nondescript college girl outfit: a white top and jeans. The other girl wore black arm sleeves and eyelash extensions. When it was her turn to report, she said she felt bored. I’m good at flirting, and it isn’t hard to get a man to sleep with you, she said. Once I start, I can see exactly where the evening will end. Here, she told me that she felt like an “apex predator.” I laughed. Then I sat there sinking into the mattress, trying to work out what the laugh was for.

It was my first time at SlutCon, a three-day retreat in Berkeley for men who wanted to get better at seduction. It was my first time at Lighthaven, the venue that hosted it. I had never been to Lighthaven, but it reminded me of my co-op at Stanford. There was an open kitchen stocked with more food than anyone could eat. People were wealthy — I mean, “high-trust” — enough to leave their laptops lying around. The sunlight was Californian cashmere on the skin. We often sat on the ground like college kids. People were visibly nude or Dionysian in places, but the atmosphere as a whole still struck me as neutered and millennial, like a hackathon that had changed its prize.

Lighthaven used to be a hotel, and it still has a hotel’s bones — it has courtyards and garden paths. Now it is operated by Lightcone Infrastructure, an organization closely associated with a subculture known as “rationalism,” which formed online in the 2000s around writers including Eliezer Yudkowsky, Robin Hanson, and now Scott Alexander. The subculture is interested in avoiding cognitive biases and applying Bayesian inferences toward real-world objectives, including artificial intelligence alignment.

Rationalism is physically instantiated as reading groups or “meet-ups” across the world, but its adherents are particularly active in Silicon Valley. They have visible discourse norms and vocabulary — “attack surface” (a total set of vulnerabilities), “priors” (a baseline), “scope insensitivity” (a cognitive bias with regard to scale). They like to measure things. Aella, a sex worker associated with the subculture and one of three founders of SlutCon, is known for running controversial online surveys querying niche sexual ethics. She is best understood as a hobbyist researcher and internet provocateur.

When I interviewed to be a flirt girl, the organizers gave me the thesis of the event: We love men (do we? I wondered) and we want men to be better at seducing us (of course). In our training, we were instructed to approach the event with high degrees of openness, along with curiosity and candor. Each flirtee would wear a wristband; when it was on, we could be approached by the attendees. People would be finding the edges of their “seduction style” over the weekend, the organizers said, so some of them would try things we might find awkward. When that happens, we should offer a gentle correction, or end the interaction by naming our intention to exit out loud. If possible, we were to avoid “crushing their spirit.”

There were roughly as many flirt girls as ticket holders. Tickets to SlutCon cost between $3,300 and $18,000, with the more expensive tickets providing limited-space workshops, personalized feedback, and what the materials called “spicier educational sessions.” While nothing in the paperwork required ticket holders to be men, or flirtees to be women, I did not meet any exceptions.

All my friends wanted to know what the SlutCon attendees were like. I told them I had never met anyone at the conference before. To my eye, the event skewed white and nebbish but not drastically so. The men I met were often rationalist or rationalist-adjacent and knew each other from previous Lighthaven events. They ranged from being in their 20s to middle-aged. They were typical heterosexual men, which is to say they conveyed a lack of style rather than having overtly bad style, though a few wore actual fedoras, like Magic the Gathering players. They were sincere and awkward, possibly Redditors, the next Pokemon evolution of the startup guys I knew in college. Some were involved in the poly and/or kink scene, and some of them were not.

The women varied more but were also largely in their mid-20s or 30s. The rationalist or rationalist-adjacent women were dressed comfortably in flannel or skater skirts like SuperWhoLock posters, and they greeted their friends wherever they went. Others were outsiders to the Lighthaven culture entirely. There was a beautiful former camgirl, who told me that Aella’s writing about escorting had described her own life. There was a sex-positive painter who had flown in for inspiration. There were two stunning housemates from another country, intrigued by the gender relations angle of the event — one wished to repair a relationship with her misogynistic brother. Somewhere in the mix was a journalist from Playboy, wearing sigil-shaped jewelry.

The crowd at SlutCon wasn’t limited to rationalists and sex workers, but both demographics were overrepresented. What everyone at the event seemed to have in common was a directness in cognitive and interpersonal style. To my surprise, I found this appealing. I’m a lawyer and am accustomed to a certain guardedness and artificiality in my professional life. For years, I’ve behaved through signs or euphemisms, like a character in an Edith Wharton novel. At SlutCon, it was fun to talk with people who would name the subtext out loud. I had a social license I usually don’t.

Theodore Gary

Theodore Gary

Long Covid

“At graduation, she was the only person wearing a mask.”

Who’s Still Masking?

Who’s Still Masking?

There are a lot of people still masking. You tend not to notice them, since their faces are covered, but they are there, always anonymous and in the background: tearing your ticket at AMC, reading on the train, shopping at the grocery store. Oftentimes they walk with a cane. You see only their eyes; it’s like looking at half a person.

I’ve seen people like this around, masked students at school with strange hair and chunky boots. I’d register their existence with curiosity but nothing more, until I discovered Maddie Blair, the 25-year-old editor of Dublin- and Chicago-based literary magazine Sabr Tooth Tiger. She posts almost daily on Instagram, and since we had both been editors-in-chief — 4 years apart — of the same arts journal at the University of Illinois, I would come across one of her posts almost every day. Who was this doe-eyed, dark-haired girl, I wondered, and why was she still posting about Covid?

Maddie is what you might call Covid-cautious (alternatively “Covid-safe,” or “anti-disease”), and it was through her Instagram I stumbled upon a constellation of Chicago-based Discord chats, mutual aid organizations, community groups, dating events, advocacy networks, Instagram pages, and even one “black centered, burlesque and drag variety show” dedicated to spreading the good word about masking, which seems to come in a package with a whole bunch of other ostensibly leftist political priorities. In July, one such organization, Clean Air Club, which distributes air-purifiers and masks, advertised three “Covid-safer” events (air purifiers on site, masks required) hosted by various organizations across the city on their Instagram: a “Somatic Healing Dance (BIPOC-only event),” a “Joy Ryde Drag Show,” and a “Book Talk with Emmaia Gelman and Summer Institute: Why We Need to #DropTheADL from Schools.” Clean Air Club is the most legitimate of these Covid-conscious organizations, boasting a profile in The Guardian and a partnership with the Illinois Department of Public Health on another July Instagram post. It felt to me that serious and strange political energies had begun to coalesce around this issue of masking, and I wanted to find out how seriously they needed to be taken.

So, on a rainy Saturday in June, I found myself accepting a flimsy cloth mask from a nice girl at the door of St. Luke’s, a simple and high-ceilinged church in the artsy Chicago neighborhood of Logan Square, where I had driven to meet Maddie and attend the launch of Sabr Tooth Tiger’s second issue. Probably 10 or 15 people had arrived by the time I walked in. One girl inched to her seat using a blue walker. Another attendee had decorated their mask with a silver chain. The church’s eight pews could have supported three, maybe four times the number of total attendees (32, at final count). Blunting the eerie emptiness were the streamers arranged in rainbow order from each wall. A number of small white boxes — air purifiers — lay scattered about.

Through a mutual friend, I had reached out to Maddie and arranged to meet her at the launch of Sabr Tooth Tiger’s second issue. She had a manic energy about her when I introduced myself. She trained her whole force of concentration on me until another person came, and then she trained it on them. Busy as Maddie was, though, she quickly ushered me over to a sweaty, balding 35-year-old, whom she introduced as Chris Rife. Rife, who typically goes by Sea, is a part of the Sabr Tooth Tiger accessibility team and a board member of Parallel Play Chicago. That organization, if you are wondering what it does, furnishes a thorough description of its mission on its website: “Parallel Play Chicago is a grassroots community organization that seeks to center the joy and liberation of COVID-cautious, LGBTQIA+, immunocompromised+ disabled individuals, and BIPOC through mutual aid, supply drives, and collaborative arts partnerships.”

I wondered what Sea thought about the CDC, about our nation’s public health authorities. It was my assumption that they would be the type to do their own research, and I was not disappointed. About Covid, Sea relies neither on the CDC’s guidance nor its research, focusing, rather, on information from “independent resources” and “papers, and syntheses of papers, and those sorts of things, too.”

“The more that we learn,” they told me, “the more that we realize that we do have the tools…there’s no better time for human beings to be living through a pandemic than right now, given the scientific advancements and the tools that we do have. There are lots of ways that we can keep people safe and keep people from spreading what is a continuing pandemic. And we just have to use the knowledge that we have and not just put our heads in the sand and pretend that everything’s normal…pretending it’s over isn’t going to make it so.”

Since my high school dropped its mask requirement in 2022, I hadn’t felt like I was pretending. The pandemic, in my life at least, was well over. St. Luke’s felt, at times, like an island in the Pacific on which a squad of Japanese soldiers carried on the Second World War long past its official expiration. Sea, at least, seemed to have a similar level of fanaticism. How could you get him to surrender, I wondered? Who would give the order?

Sea and Maddie first bonded over being among the few in the Chicago alternative literary scene who continued masking after the pandemic’s official end. “For a while I was trying to continue doing what I was doing but wearing a mask,” Sea told me. “And it always was a lonely experience of being, like, the only masked person at an event, especially in rooms where you felt like you’ve always kind of belonged prior to that and then this kind of feeling of othering that happens when you are the only person doing it.” Together, Sea and Maddie hatched the idea for Sabr Tooth Tiger, a magazine that not only took masking seriously but integrated it into the publication’s mission. Every Sabr Tooth Tiger event is mask-required. “It is possible to take precautions and keep people safe, and also go to poetry readings, and do readings yourself, and have conversations, and all those sorts of things,” Sea told me.

Sea stopped short of proposing a return to the masking regime of July 2020 during our chat, but they never ruled it out, either, and I got the sneaking suspicion that it would not necessarily be unwelcome. “The only thing that really changed was the government response to it,” Sea told me. “And so I have a lot of friends who are, you know, compromised, and the risks that other people might take are not things that they can do, including going to live events and things like that…in the same way I don’t want to get sick going to a poetry reading, I don’t want somebody who has to go to work at a restaurant to get sick just because they have to get a paycheck and pay rent. I think we all truly deserve clean air in the way that we all truly deserve clean water. The great news is that we have the tools to do it. It’s just a matter of having the cultural will.”

Eli Goldfine

Eli Goldfine

High School or Claude?

on self-educating through AI

AI in 8th Grade

AI in 8th Grade

This summer I heard various rumors coming out of Manifest (the prediction market conference held annually in Berkeley) that an unusually young kid named Eli Goldfine was wandering the Lighthaven grounds. The 14-year-old, I was told, had traveled there with his dad to interview Robin Hanson, the peculiar economist and prediction market forefather. Eli had also recently gotten into a fight with his middle school’s administration for betting on Manifold (the playmoney market that hosts Manifest) that he’d win co-chair in his class election (Eli won). And, most curiously, so the rumor went, Sam Bankman-Fried’s parents now wanted Eli to manage their jailed son’s Twitter account.

The 9th grader from Westchester, NY is part of the first wave of AI-conscious wunderkinds, self-starters without facial hair who, in the parlance of Silicon Valley, just build, learn, and do things. Eli hosts The Supercycle, a podcast on prediction markets, one of his many projects (e.g. coordinating underutilized, consumer-grade Seestar telescopes to perform follow-ups on certain objects that big, fancy, completely-booked telescopes can’t).

As Eli tells it, his edge is that, unlike his peers playing sports or video games, he cares about things that actually matter (philosophy, government, economics, astronomy, AI, prediction markets) — and not just for reasons of parental expectation or social status.

Eli is a precocious fellow, certainly, but he also represents the future of learning: self-education through AI. Eli started high school a few days after we spoke in August, much to his own chagrin. “If I had good AI ed tech, I could get through high school in a year or less,” Eli said on Liron Shapira’s podcast Doom Debates. “I don’t have any domain expertise in software engineering in the slightest.” He then described his workflow on various projects as “basically alternating between Claude, Codex, Twitter, and Substack all day...I’ve [just] never hit a wall where I need a human to go and do something.”

Born circa 2012, Eli forewarns of a world very different from the one most of us grew up in. In Eli’s world, one does not wait around to learn, or languish in their passivity, or loiter until they’re 18 to start companies. There’s no excuse, really — who cares about pedigree or status in a world of unlimited agency and action? Eli stands in opposition to the prophecy that AI will demolish young minds through the outsourcing of intelligence. As you’ll see in our interview, there has never been a better time to be an autodidact.

Should Eli go to high school? When did he realize he could learn more through Claude than class? What was the campaign platform that won him his middle school election? What are the prospects for his cohort in a post-AGI/ASI age?

How did Eli find the George Mason University economists? What’s the scale of his telescope project? How did Eli lose his playmoney trying to insider trade on Manifold? What does he think of Kalshi and Polymarket? Will prediction markets ever realize their full, epistemic potential?

How did Eli nearly end up on SBF’s prison contact list? What made Manifest “way weirder” than Eli thought? What did Eli’s dad make of the rationalists?

Should we implement futarchy? What should humanity’s sacred goal be? What are Eli’s long-term aspirations? What does he think of San Francisco? Does thinking about big ideas provoke any existentialism in Eli?

Will Diana

Will Diana

MrBeast, Slop Auteur

“According to the memo, MrBeast’s art justifies all — there is no reason to live, it seems, except to make a MrBeast video.”

The Art of YouTube

The Art of YouTube

Would you do what it takes for wealth and fame? Would you humiliate, debase, and torture yourself for a shot at stardom? There is a man who has done what it takes to become rich and famous, and he now tirelessly uses his wealth and fame to put other people in humiliating, debasing, and torturous situations for their own opportunities at success. Before that, though, he was a nobody with a dream. His dream was YouTube fame, and the only way he could achieve this dream was through understanding its algorithm.

Raised an evangelical by a single mother in Greenville, North Carolina, he was an introvert with consuming obsessions. As a youth, his obsessions were split between YouTube and baseball. He even hoped to become a MLB player. But this idea was crushed when he was diagnosed at the age of 15 with Crohn’s disease. The strain this condition put on his body forced him to give up on baseball and retreat indoors. He saw potential in online video creators who were starting to make real money in brand deals: YouTube would be his salvation.

He soon joined a group of other minor YouTubers who spent 10 hours a day studying how to go viral. He learned how to make the optimal title and thumbnail, along with hundreds of other minute aspects of editing, lighting, and pacing that gain and maintain attention. But despite his efforts, the algorithm was cruel. By the age of 19, after seven years of toil, he had been lucky enough to make a few dollars. He ceased to care about money, or art, or even love. He cared only about YouTube.

But after an entire youth wasted, after being unable to speak to kids at school about anything other than YouTube — and even then, his obsession for the topic often drove everyone away from discussing it with him — after dropping out of community college and being kicked out of his home by a mother who knew in her heart that her son was ruining his God-given life by spending it on a website dominated by children and gamers, the young man was finally about to become somebody. Grimacing, he sat in his chair, turned on the camera, and spoke.

“I’m about to count to 100,000. If you don’t believe me, just watch this video. All I want to say is, just Tweet the video out, share it with maybe Keem or Scarce, and if you’re a YouTuber, just help a guy out. 1 Think of the pain I’m about to go through — screw it. Let’s just — let’s. One.”

As he started counting, did he know? So mastered by the brute power of the algorithm, was he aware of what was to come? Did he see the hordes of people chanting his name, the cities he would build? Allegedly, he only remembers saying “one” — the remaining 999,999 numbers passed by like a bad dream. Regardless of whatever he dreamed after inflicting 40 hours of torture on himself, the young man said 100,000 and collapsed into his chair. Born Jimmy Donaldson in 1997, he had, with this act, officially crowned himself before the world with his true title: MrBeast.

Jimmy Donaldson uploaded “I Counted To 100,000!” on January 9, 2017. As of 2026, he is a billionaire. His main MrBeast YouTube channel has over 500 million subscribers, representing 6% of the world population. This account is the most subscribed-to YouTube channel in the world, and this is not counting MrBeast Gaming, Beast Philanthropy, Beast Reacts, MrBeast 2, and Beast Animations. His reality TV show, Beast Games, is Amazon’s most viewed unscripted show — Beast Games had the most contestants in reality television history (1,000) and the biggest cash-prize ($5,000,000). He’s a philanthropist who has dug wells, healed the blind, and planted trees; he has spent seven days buried alive in a coffin, seven days in solitary confinement, and seven days in a cave. He’ll do anything for content, damnit.

After counting to 100,000, MrBeast received a brand deal for $10,000 from a now-defunct NFT marketplace. He was 19 years old; he could have bought nice clothes, or invested the money, or thrown a big party — which is probably what I would have done. He could have bought better camera equipment — which is what any other self-serious YouTube grinder-entrepreneur probably would have done. Instead, MrBeast did something truly savvy. He stuffed all $10,000 in an envelope, gave it to a panhandler, and filmed it the whole time — that’s late-capitalist Jesus Christ right there! The shifty freak has a supernatural ability to sniff out content. He’ll do something absurd and attention-grabbing, and then, once he has the attention of millions, advertisers will flock to pay him; finally, with the money from advertising, he’ll fund another striking exploit. By constantly trapping the viewer in an incessant, hyperactive, compulsive cycle, the MrBeast machine — get attention, get investments, pump that into the next scheme, and constantly refine, reinvest, and compete — hurtles forward.

Watching a MrBeast video, though, you, too, start to get hungry; you want to compete. Though his challenges require no skill, or capital, or even intelligence — only determination and a willingness to humiliate oneself — you are compelled to ask yourself, What would I do for this money, this fame, this salvation? Could I stand in a circle for hours, or spend months of my life without leaving a grocery store, or count to 100,000 nonstop?

MrBeast’s competitions — like his real life “Squid Game” with 456 contestants, a $456,000 prize, and an accurate reproduction of the Korean Netflix show, minus the killing — are massive productions. But his challenges, in which people dare to withstand absurd situations like living in a grocery store, spending 100 days in a red circle, or spending 100 days in a private jet, for monetary rewards, tend to be his most ridiculous videos. “Last To Leave Grocery Store, Wins $250,000” is emblematic of this category. In it, the Beast buys a grocery store in his hometown of Greenville, North Carolina and announces a 50%-off sale, thus enticing a discount-hungry crowd into the store. Once it is full, MrBeast announces over a megaphone that the last person to leave the grocery store will win $250,000 — they can use anything in the grocery store to their advantage, but they can’t leave.

The Striver Class

“Just as I saw the social ladder as a kind of ethnography, my other classmates saw it as a winnable game. And it is winnable, that is the unspeakable thrill of it.”

The Law School Elite

The Law School Elite

I’m worried nostalgia is a fascist emotion, I once announced to my law school housemate, a man who was forcefully subjected to my internal monologue for over two years. Gideon would consider my claim while reheating his leftovers. So is hunger, he’d rejoin, gesturing at the microwave. Then I would go upstairs and be nostalgic anyway.

I recently graduated from one of the top law schools in the United States. While I was there, I became terribly nostalgic for my childhood. It wasn’t because I had a good childhood. I grew up in a troubled household in New Zealand. Neither of my parents went to college; my grandparents are illiterate. We were constantly in debt, and everyone in my family blamed each other for it. Nothing about my upbringing involved unusual disadvantage, but I don’t think I met anyone else at my law school whose parents owed them money. People like Gideon were far more common there; his grandfather was an alum, and he had parents in academia. So my nostalgia puzzled me at first, because I was deeply unhappy in New Zealand. But after law school, I realized I missed reading the phrase “making the world a better place” without experiencing its mandatory sarcastic aftertaste. I missed not knowing how power really worked.

A selective law school is simultaneously serious and unserious. It’s a trade school, but it’s also a finishing school. In the United States, it is often a pipeline to the political class, so it has to be taken seriously as a culture; simultaneously, non-interdisciplinary legal academia is a joke, and law reviews may be the most embarrassing form of knowledge production on the planet. When you enter a selective law school, the world you come to reside in becomes extraordinarily parochial. I attended an elite institution as an undergraduate, too, but even a college with billionaires still has thousands of students majoring in diverse fields — the population is large enough to disappear into. Elite law schools permit no such disappearance. Mine had the class size of a high school and the claustrophobic social dynamics to match.

Because everyone is entering adjacent rungs of the same profession, there is the ugly sense that everyone might know everyone, forever. When I intern at an organization across the country, middle-aged staff attorneys ask me how my professors are doing. When I visit one friend at Oxford, another friend’s ex-boyfriend is in the same PhD cohort. When I go to dinner with anyone from Princeton, they jokingly threaten to FaceTime my failed talking stage who went there, too. And because this world is so insular, people behave in ways that are extraordinarily repellent to any normal person. Everyone is reasonably smart — they write solid papers that make incremental claims, or they’re Rhodes Scholars. They also have a pathetic need for validation that comes from being too good too young, and most will spend their entire lives reinforcing the status quo.

There was a game that I largely didn’t play but was acutely aware of as a law student: secret dinners with Supreme Court justices, six-figure book deals, penthouse parties, private island visits, appellate clerkships secretly offered in the spring semester of our first year. Because I was foreign, and therefore politically irrelevant, I could watch this unfold as one watches reality TV. My ongoing “bit” with Gideon was that of a well-meaning but bigoted anthropologist dispatched from my country to record the customs of the American ruling class. Certain professors and law students ought to be brought back to my civilization, I suggested, to be exhibited. Because everyone was competitive, ludicrously granular kinds of hierarchy emerged. One professor taught a seminar on nobility, advocating directly for the “aristocratic” notion that some human beings are superior at the art of living. Several professors refused to hire research assistants who hadn’t attended Harvard, Yale, Princeton, Stanford or MIT (HYPSM) as undergraduates. One professor was banned from partaking in the admissions process altogether because he would simply rate any applicant who hadn’t gone to Harvard a 0.

Every time I returned to New Zealand, I found it increasingly difficult to explain what law school was like. My mother might ask me what classes I was taking this semester, and I might say that I was taking Federal Courts. But I wasn’t taking Federal Courts. I was bearing witness to Biblical hubris. The class was taught by an infamous professor perpetually dressed in a pooling suit; I often joked that he needed to be gently vacuumed. He would compare himself to Jesus, without being Kanye. He spent most of his lectures seething about how his brother had clerked for the Supreme Court instead of him. He would name-drop past teaching assistants of his who had ascended to the Solicitor General’s office, he would applaud himself for not having a chauffeur. He would refer to lower court judges as “automata.” And for ideological reasons, this professor refused to teach habeas (a petition used to challenge the legality of detention), advocating that all we needed to know is that we should deny them when we clerked. The class collectively assembled a “bingo card” for these pet topics.

This is torture for someone as bitchily irrepressible as I am. You can’t laugh, because these people run America. You have to laugh, because these people are flagrantly ridiculous. Many of my classmates and professors did not regularly interact with people outside their social class; their brains cannot proportion risk. They agonize over the prestige gap between Wachtell and Simpson Thacher, two corporate firms whose differences are only perceptible from inside the terrarium. They scoff at the idea of clerking on the Fourth Circuit, a job most law graduates in the country might light a candle for.

Just as I saw the social ladder as a kind of ethnography, my other classmates saw it as a winnable game. And it is winnable, that is the unspeakable thrill of it. You can go to this law school, and later become the president, or a Supreme Court justice — many people have done this before. But opportunities for ascension are not transparently awarded. If your grandparents were alumni, you arrived knowing this — I had to make sad eyes at upperclassmen until they relented and told me. Only some professors could offer you Power, and they didn’t offer you Power in exchange for work. You were either anointed with love, or you weren’t. One professor explicitly compared the legal profession’s client-patronage system to racehorse pedigrees; he was mentored by Owen Fiss, a famous constitutional law scholar, so his fursona (he wouldn’t call it that) was Seabiscuit. He referred to his favorite students as the future Abraham Lincolns and Frederick Douglasses.

But once you acquire anything on the basis of nepotism, you can lose these things on the basis of interpersonal meddling, too; my classmates viciously doxxed each other. When conservatives snitched on others they deemed insufficiently Catholic, clerkships were rescinded, and jobs were lost. The result was an eerie social environment organized around ostentatious de-risking. Decades in advance, people were fanatically pruning away behavior that might complicate a confirmation hearing. Some of my classmates would not dance or drink at socials. Some carried burner phones abroad, they were so paranoid about surveillance.

My friend Adam was the gentlest case. In our second year, I texted him a question I considered weightless: was Professor R. a good lecturer, or should I take “Administrative Law” with someone else, instead? The typing bubble surfaced and vanished several times. Then he asked, Are you alone? I was alone, and my phone rang. “I’m sorry, I don’t want to put that kind of thing in writing,” he told me . Put what in writing? “My opinion,” he’d added with the patience of someone explaining fire to a child. Adam may want to be a judge one day.

Manifest Man

“At Manifest, though, there is a certain existential loneliness, a specifically sexual strain of angst, that did not lift once in the three days of the conference.”

Rationalist Workshop

Rationalist Workshop

On a cool June evening in Berkeley, I watched a man named Victor try to shoot a beam of light out of his penis. Minutes earlier, he had raised his hand because he found the volunteer onstage before him attractive. And now here he was, facing her in front of a crowd of perhaps 60 people, having been instructed to do precisely this by a woman named Aella, a pseudonymous camgirl and self-described sex researcher. She had promised the men in the room that the exercise, if undertaken in earnest, might actually result in hookups, real ones. Now she told her first subject to imagine himself gathering all of the energy in his body into his pelvis and then sending that energy outward as a beam of light, straight through his trousers and into the room.

Victor pointed out that this seemed a little absurd, which it manifestly was. But he did it anyway, standing there and trying — and you could see him trying — to imagine himself emitting light from the tip of his penis. Aella reported that Victor wasn’t shooting enough light, and he readjusted. She and the volunteer watched. The rest of us did, too. And then the volunteer delivered her verdict, which was that Victor had come up short. She had, in fact, “felt more” from him a moment earlier, before he’d begun to imagine light streaming out of his phallus.

This was Manifest, and Victor’s ordeal belonged to its official programming. The conference — this was its fourth iteration — convenes each summer at Lighthaven, a verdant complex of gardens and halls in a converted Berkeley hotel that rationalists keep as a gathering place. At Manifest, rationalism has little to do with Descartes; it’s a Bay Area subculture built around the site LessWrong, a “community blog” preoccupied with mathematics, philosophy, genetics, and the apocalyptic risks (and opportunities) presented by artificial intelligence.

Around 800 people attend Manifest each year. It takes its name, and its nominal subject, from Manifold, a prediction market. At the opening assembly, Austin Chen, co-founder of Manifold, asked everyone who had ever bet on it to stand, and very nearly the whole audience got to its feet. Officially, then, this is a conference about forecasting. But “a conference about prediction markets” describes Manifest about as well as “a conference about effigies” would describe Burning Man. Prediction markets are what the attendees have in common, but they are not, mostly, what they came to discuss.

Any attendee could propose a session on any topic throughout the weekend, and several hundred sessions took place over the three days, a dozen or so underway in any given hour. At one session, attendees proposed political systems that might replace representative democracy (among them “futarchy,” a governance framework in which voters set overarching goals and prediction markets determine the specific policies used to achieve them). At another, a married couple gave a practical guide to IQ-screening one’s unborn children, drawn from their own experience doing the same. At the very moment that I watched Victor try and fail to emit photons from his manhood, a few doors down, a mathematician was explaining his PhD thesis on the topology of three-dimensional shapes.

Aella’s session was titled Get Hotter With Aella (Reinforcement Learning: Hot Girl Feedback). Reinforcement learning with human feedback is a technique for teaching a machine learning model to do what a human wants it to do. The model produces an output, a human rewards or penalizes it, and the cycle repeats, each round nudging the machine’s behavior closer to what the human prefers. Here, the model was Victor, and Aella, the human in the loop, was teaching him to be desired.

It didn’t work. Victor left the stage no closer to seducing his woman of choice. Round after round, the men failed. Now another man, Alex, raised his hand to face a new woman, Sam, while the room looked on. Alex’s trouble, Aella determined, was his stiffness; he was holding himself like he was bracing for a flu shot.

So she set about loosening him. “Tense your abdomen,” she told him. “I want large circles.” Alex made the circles with his arms, but Sam reported that he still felt “very stiff” to her. Everything about him, Sam added, was “feeling very robotic.”

Then Aella told Alex to touch Sam. “Reach out,” she said, “and touch Sam in a way that feels okay.” Alex smiled, a wide and sudden smile, and swung his arm up and over Sam’s shoulders in a single great swoop, planting his hand at the base of her neck, his face fixed in an awkward rictus.

“Let’s put that hand down,” Aella said. “Now let’s try it again. Step closer.” Alex stepped closer and reached for Sam a second time. Sam reported that everything about it still felt “very robotic.”

Luddite Club

“I haven’t remotely gone full-force into Luddism. Despite that, I’m here in New York at the Summer of Ludd to sing, and dance, and philosophize with the rest of them.”

To Phone or Not?

To Phone or Not?

I am midway down South Street, phone in hand and footsteps fast. Every time I walk down this strip of sidewalk, I think of the time during freshman year when my friends peed somewhere along this street — wherever there was some small shred of privacy to be had — their Halloween costumes not nearly warm enough in the nippy fall air.

I am walking with my phone held in front of me, eyes on the solid blue line leading the way, looking up from Apple Maps to catch the snow, the frost dusting the concrete, remembering that Penn Museum is here, I think, noticing that there is some sun out, and it is illuminating a vaguely collegiate building past the intersection. I follow my phone like it is a shepherd. I remind myself that I am going somewhere new. As I cross S 33rd St, I pass itinerant figures heading in the same direction, some bunching at the intersection as I walk past, others speaking on the phone, someone loudly saying something about changing her mind.

I am cold but not that cold. I am too-aware of the block of earth metals in my hand that is receiving the brunt of my attention — only because I am following its directions, but still, it is ironic. I am slightly nervous because I have only ever seen the person that I am meeting in a picture from a New York Times article. I am walking into a coffee shop. I am meeting Biruk Watling, one of the original members of the New York Luddite Club (NYLC).

My mother scrolls Facebook in the passenger seat of the car, on the couch, in bed. I judge her for it, and then I open YouTube Shorts. Recently, she instated a new rule, one we never had as kids: phones in the kitchen by midnight. Last month, as I was plugging in my phone in the kitchen, I told my brother I wished the rule was for 11 o’clock rather than midnight. He said I could put my phone away then, no one’s stopping me. I said, “I know.”

We all talk about being addicted to our phones, but as far as I’ve heard, “addiction” is a term used casually, lightly, self-deprecatingly — like it’s simply an everyday practice that practically cannot be helped. It feels this way (bad, but not bad enough to feel agony over) partly because it seems like everyone does it. If phone and social media use is an addiction, one that prompts occasional invocations from our parents to give it up, these urges have felt more and more hollow of late.

The three winners of my school’s No Phone Society challenge lasted for a total of 79 days without their phones. I participated last year, my freshman spring at Swarthmore College, for exactly three days and seven hours before my tennis team traveled to Pittsburgh for the weekend. Even for those who lasted for months, the challenge ended eventually. The participants’ phones were returned to them. Life moved on.

In January, after combing the internet for her contact information and coming up blank, I slid into Watling’s LinkedIn DMs. Luddites like Watling, a junior at Temple University, are nearly impossible to get a hold of. I knew about the Luddites from the New York Times article that inspired me to write a high school feature in which I went phoneless for one day. My tone in the piece veered from sensational to insipid. (To open, I described my high school as a “hot spot for throngs of teens bent over tiny glowing screens,” and I concluded, “I’m not actually that obsessed with my phone.”) The New York Luddite Club was formed sometime before 2022 by high schoolers looking to liberate themselves from technology and the tech oligarchs who control it; notably, many of these original club members replaced their smartphones with flip phones.

I had forgotten about the Luddites until winter break of my sophomore year. I was home from college, and I was bored. It had been over a year since I deleted Instagram; I deactivated my Instagram accounts in November 2024, during my first semester at Swarthmore. I’d joined Perfectly Imperfect (an app based around sharing recommendations) and started reading more on Substack and writing on there a bit, too. On these ostensibly “alternative” social media apps, it felt like everyone was talking about wanting to “go analog.” I remembered the Luddites, not the 19th-century ones but the high schoolers, and when I googled them, I saw The New York Times had published another piece. The Luddite cause had been made collegiate, the original members creating individual Luddite groups at colleges and cities scattered across the United States. Watling’s name and photo was front and center. Apparently, she went to school in Philadelphia. I lived outside Philly.

Watling responded to my LinkedIn message by saying that she and the co-leader of the Philadelphia Luddite Club had taken a step back and that they were looking for someone to restructure it. I didn’t have the time to run the club myself, but I wanted to join it, if there was still a club to join. I didn’t know how to make that clear over text, but I didn’t need to; Watling gave me her phone number, and we decided to meet for coffee in the city.

If you asked me right now what I like most about Instagram, I would probably say nothing; my tendencies veer toward the offline, even if I don’t always satisfy them. But if I thought about it for a second, there are a few things I would say I like about Instagram. I might say something about the sociological potential of Reels, or Instagram’s easily accessible political momentum and community, or the utility with which one can find new music or interesting art. Then again, I never saw much cool art or discovered much new music on Instagram, the politics are a shitshow, and Reels are mind-numbing (though perhaps nominally useful to a sociologist with extremely strong self-control and a chemical inability to experience dopamine spikes).

Jacob Zucker

Jacob Zucker

The Blackpill

“Where does this darkness come from? Contemporary anomie has many sources, and it is felt most deeply by those who feel ‘ongezellig.’”

Internet Terrorism

Internet Terrorism

In May, 18-year-old Caleb Vazquez walked into the Islamic Center of San Diego with a gun. He and a friend, 17-year-old Cain Clark, shot and killed three men named Amin Abdullah, Nadir Awad, and Mansour Kaziha. Soon after, they killed themselves.

Caleb and Cain wrote a 75-page manifesto titled The New Crusade: Sons of Tarrant. The title honors Brenton Tarrant, the Australian whose own 74-page manifesto, The Great Replacement, preceded the murder of 51 people at two mosques in Christchurch in 2019.

There’s a photo of Caleb that’s been floating around the internet, in which he has taken a bite out of a stroopwafel and is holding a plush of Mymy, a character from the online animated series Ongezellig.

Ongezellig is not a landmark in animation. Dutch animator Sam Tollenaar made it alone, over four years, during evenings stolen from his day job at the public broadcaster BNNVARA. The whole thing runs 24 minutes across six episodes. In those 24 minutes, Tollenaar tells the story of three adoptive sisters and their upcoming presentation for history class.

What about this anime-style Dutch cartoon led to its immense popularity within a niche, racist corner of the internet?

Let’s start with the show’s title. “Gezelligheid” is a Dutch word said to resist translation, although “conviviality” comes closest. It names the warmth of an inviting space, the social ease that a high-trust society runs on. The adjective form is “gezellig.”

“Ongezellig,” on the other hand, refers to those things that are not “gezellig” — think a situation that is uninviting, or a person who is standoffish. We could translate it as “unsociable,” or “uncozy.”

Ongezellig’s lead, Maya, is one such “unsociable” figure. She is of Dutch-Indonesian-Surinamese-Chinese-Indian descent and grew up in Belgium. She has ADD and becomes immensely flustered whenever she has to interact with anyone. She has two friends, but they are imaginary. Maya is racked with fear that her confident, charming adoptive sister Coco, who is from South Africa, will notice her lack of friends and ask her about it.

She ponders suicide. She does not kill herself. She does very little of anything in the show besides watch tentacle porn and write the words “geschiedenis van belgie,” or “history of Belgium,” at the top of a Word document.

Caleb’s heart, though, belonged to Mymy, a fervent Dutch nationalist adopted from Japan. She wears colored contact lenses, dyes her hair red, and denies her Japanese heritage. When Coco begins to tell their teacher that Mymy is from Japan, Mymy cuts her off and claims to be from “Japsterdam.”

Benjamin Samuels

Benjamin Samuels

What Was College For?

The winning address of the first New Critic essay contest

Dark Academia

Dark Academia

I have not lived for a very long time, but I have already made a handful of decisions which I deeply regret, among them my decision to write an article about Deep Springs College, my alma mater, called “What’s Better Than Harvard? A Year of Honest Work” for The Free Press. The article took me no more than a day or two, and when it was published, I received several thousand dollars.

Naturally, I would have written the article for free. It was a good writing credit. More importantly, it was an opportunity to burnish my school’s reputation. This responsibility was uniquely mine: at the time, I chaired Deep Springs’ Communications Committee and was tasked with broadcasting the college’s existence and merits to the rest of the world.

If you haven’t heard of Deep Springs, then (unfortunately for the Communications Committee) you are in the vast majority of Americans. The college receives only a few hundred applications per year, and once the Applications Committee is finished with its preliminary cull, only a few dozen serious applicants remain. Intense deliberation follows among the members of the Applications Committee, often stretching for multiple hours into the night, out of which emerge 13 ranked contenders and a short waitlist. At the eleventh hour, a few accepted students typically withdraw their applications in horror or indecision, and two or three students on the waitlist are tapped to take their place.

The finalized class is flown into Bishop, California and bussed an hour into the Sierra Nevada to a barren valley twice the size of Manhattan, with an abandoned prospecting settlement at its north end and a low-lying swamp, politely known as Deep Springs Lake, in the south. The college takes up a few square acres of irrigated land near the center, encircled by high, jagged mountains that rise steeply out of nothing. The valley itself is perfectly flat, smoothed by the northward passage of the glaciers at the end of the last Ice Age.

I will spare you the remaining details of this peculiar institution, since they have been told and retold with very little variation many times already — by students in The New Yorker and The London Times, as well as by professional journalists at CBS, The Economist, The Guardian, The Huffington Post, The Financial Times, Vanity Fair, Smithsonian Magazine, and, most recently, The New York Times (in addition to my own feature for The Free Press). You can pick any of these pieces to read at random, as the authors substantially agree with one another, although they respectfully space their coverage at three- or four-year intervals.

It was as the head of the Communications Committee, engaged in facilitating a visit by The Financial Times, that I first noticed this pattern. Whenever journalists visited the college, the article always seemed to turn out well. For instance, in 2009, as the college’s refusal to admit women became increasingly anomalous, Vanity Fair had written admiringly in “Cowboy Scholars” of the “academically elite college where 26 male students work a 2,500-acre cattle ranch.” After Deep Springs went co-ed in 2018, The Guardian shrugged, “[this] strange, beguiling institution in a desert valley where human purpose is debated amid coyotes and cows…will change, but perhaps not by much.”

And always you found in these articles the hatred of modernity and the handwringing about a “collapse of public trust” and a “castration of attention spans” — generously spiced, of course, with assurances that Deep Springs is “the most selective small university in the world,” that its students have an “average SAT score of 1500,” and that “many will transfer to the Ivy League.”

In the public imagination, Deep Springs was the best of both worlds. It was everything that everything else was not; it could not lose. So several months after Covid, as the outside world briefly turned its full attention towards cancel culture, I was pleased but not surprised when The Financial Times released its own report: “The U.S. College Where There Are No Culture Wars.”

I suspect that part of what makes Deep Springs so vulnerable to interpretation is the gaping hole at the college’s heart, a negative space which, elsewhere, is occupied by careerism. True, Deep Springers often find their way back toward New York City, and San Francisco, and Washington, D.C. But within the valley they are expected to keep their futures fastidiously blank. L.L. Nunn, the hydroelectric tycoon who founded Deep Springs in 1917, famously declared that his school would prepare graduates to “lead a life of service.” Yet what kind of service L.L. Nunn had in mind is not at all clear from his gnostic letters and writings, published as The Grey Book and distributed to every incoming class with a wink — as if for ambitious, well-educated Americans, blacksmithing or carpentry could be anything other than a pathetic self-indulgence.

So at Deep Springs the word “service” has been taken to imply something narrower. Namely, a humbling through work, and more specifically, ranch work: riding, herding, sorting, feeding, milking, branding, and slaughter — which is all unbelievably romantic. It is embarrassingly difficult for anyone, myself included, to shake the stubborn apprehension that they have stepped onto a movie set.

Jasmine Sun

Jasmine Sun

Jasmine Sun’s Project of Self-Transformation

on Sontag, Stanford, and Silicon Valley

Becoming a Tech Journalist

Becoming a Tech Journalist

Jasmine Sun is the author of the popular Substack “Jasmine’s Substack.” She is a contributing writer to The Atlantic, has published multiple pieces in The New York Times, and was recently interviewed by Ezra Klein. Her beat is the technologies and social mores of Silicon Valley. In her writing about Chinese peptides, the “permanent underclass,” and the furor over the construction of data centers, she has become the go-to “anthropologist of disruption.” She is 26.

“I’m only interested in people engaged in a project of self-transformation,” Susan Sontag wrote in her journals. Jasmine connected with that quote immediately upon reading it: she has been engaged in that project for a long-time. She joined the 826 writing seminars at 8-years-old, and was a champion high-school debater. At Stanford, she realized that the start-up world was a matter more of knowing the language than anything else, so she read the Silicon Valley canon. When she couldn’t get a job as a journalist, she started work at Substack, eventually becoming a project manager leading the core product team, before resigning to write full-time.

In her advice to college graduates of the class of 2026, Jasmine writes: “The old world was bad. Those staid institutions and rigid hierarchies are not worth mourning.” We can no longer expect that going to the right schools and checking the right boxes guarantees a life of wealth and flourishing; that world is gone. In this world where Substack, San Francisco, and AI all determine our future, we all have something to learn from Jasmine Sun.

I, unfortunately, did a lot of competitive debate growing up, so this is probably a big part of why I feel reasonably comfortable speaking on podcasts. I spent a lot of time doing the kind of debate in high school where you talk about critical theory at 300 words per minute. I feel like everybody in that community senses an affinity with others — I can name all of the other writers who used to be policy debaters off the top of my head. Ben Lerner did Policy, Sally Rooney did British Parliamentary, Nate Silver was a Policy debater, Jay Caspian Kang was a Policy debater, Kelsey Piper was a Policy debater, and Jerusalem Demsas debated, too.

That probably helped a lot with getting good at making arguments orally without having everything written down and thought-through beforehand — it’s bullshitting, frankly. You just learn to be really good at bullshitting when you’re 14 years old. One skill that I’m unusually good at relative to other people, which is not a very interesting superpower, is cross-examination. I love being asked hard questions. Before I was a writer, I worked at Substack, and I loved doing town hall events where everyone was angry and asking, “Why are you ruining my app? Why would you introduce video to Substack? Why would you introduce a social feed?” It was super fun to think about hard questions and try to get good answers.

I always really enjoyed being cross-examined, and a podcast is just a very long cross-examination.

One of the things that makes people incredibly charismatic, whether you’re talking about Susan Sontag, or Bernie Sanders, or Steve Jobs, is they might be assholes — they might not even be that smart or that correct a lot of the time — but charisma comes, in part, purely from the sense that this person is acting in total accordance with their will — there is no separate inner and outer self. And I think that Sontag, and Steve Jobs, and, you know, our most charismatic politicians and business leaders, do embody that. I don’t think charisma is the only thing that matters — I don’t think charisma is the same as virtue — but I do find that really interesting.

People on the East Coast in media love to ask me, “Why are they talking about killing everybody with AI? Why are you trying to sell your product by saying it’s gonna take everybody’s job and go rogue and commit a cybercrime,” or whatever? Part of this is that Dario Amodei really, really believes that AI might cause permanent runaway inequality, and also that it might cause a bioterrorist attack that kills several million people. And I think that there is charisma that attracts a lot of these “autistic” AI researchers to working with Dario, because this guy has a unity of conscience and will and action. He is saying exactly the thing that is within him. It’s not charismatic in the sense of sort of a normal, likable, I-would-grab-a-beer-with-him thing. It’s kind of the opposite of that. But the charisma comes from this sense that he is fully, authentically himself, and he’s that committed to his cause. But then it causes problems, of course.

Sam Altman, for example, for a long time was considered incredibly, incredibly charismatic. That’s how he was always able to fail upward: from his failed start-up, to being president of YC, and then kind of fired from YC, to OpenAI, to being fired from OpenAI, to coming back even more powerful than ever. It’s like, how does this guy keep failing up? And it’s because people in tech and AI consider him very charismatic and very relationally competent, in a way that certainly none of the rest of the world thinks of Sam Altman. He does, though, have a reality distortion field around him in the same way, so that when he talks about AI, it is imbued with a sense of existential weight, and people really sense that he believes that the future could be that different, and that great, or that awe-inspiring. People just sense that in Sam Altman’s future, the world could look very different. When they’re around him, they get excited by that. I don’t think that excites a lot of people, but it excites people in the AI world.

It would be really great if, by 2030, I felt like I was, in my head, the best tech journalist. It’s unclear what this means. It’s totally undefined. I need to win tech journalism by 2030, and then I will switch careers. And I don’t know what I’ll do. My assumption is just that if I win, I will be bored, and then I will want to do something else. Maybe I’ll get really into writing fiction. I’ve never really written fiction since I was a kid. Maybe I’ll go back into the tech industry. Maybe I’ll be really interested in philanthropy. I have no idea. I don’t really care. It’s not that deep.

Present at the Creation

on documenting the Singularity

Monitoring the Situation

Monitoring the Situation

Two years ago, the chief-of-staff to Anthropic’s CEO declared, “These next five years might be the last few years that I work.” At the time, she spoke for a world that knows far more about the future than the average American. But even before the release of ChatGPT, Theo Jaffee knew that the future was happening in the West. The 21-year-old University of Florida drop-out found his computer science classes in Gainesville pointless; they operated under old assumptions about how to build a career. Come summertime, he left for San Francisco, drawing on connections with former Curtis Yarvin intern Stevie Miller, attending the Manifest conference in Berkeley, and building out his Twitter following. Now Jaffee is the co-founder of Monitoring The Situation (MTS), an Andreesen-Horowitz backed media company that streams interviews of central players in AI and technology all day on X (formerly Twitter). Jaffee is San Francisco’s go-to reporter and AGI discussant, tirelessly cataloguing, describing, and perhaps influencing the future of our world.

A Spanish ruler declared long ago, “Had I been present at the Creation, I would have given some useful hints for the better ordering of the universe.” But if you cannot be present at the creation — well, at least you can monitor the situation. Below, I talk to Jaffee about becoming “AGI-pilled” and what we should do to prepare for a superintelligence we’re all underestimating.

This was my freshman year of college. I didn’t have an internship for that summer, so I decided — kind of like one of these people I knew from Twitter, Dwarkesh Patel — I would start a podcast where I’d find people I liked on Twitter and interview them. This was summer of 2023, three years ago now. I started interviewing a few people. My first guest was Greg Fodor. Some of the more famous people I interviewed were Zvi Mowshowitz, Robin Hanson, Bryan Caplan, and so on. I did maybe 20 episodes over the two years of the podcast — I definitely should have done more.

In August 2023, I visited SF for the first time. I didn’t meet any mutuals then, but I discovered the city and fell in love with the place. I was like, “Wow. It’s beautiful, it’s full of technology and tech people — I definitely need to be here after college.” I don’t love the city as much anymore, but I still love the people.

Throughout my sophomore year — fall 2023 through spring 2024 — I continued being really interested in AI and AGI. This was the GPT-4 Turbo era, and then Claude 3 Opus came out around that time, too. I continued reading Yarvin and other right-wing people like Richard Hanania. That summer — May 2024 — I again didn’t have an internship. I had a few thousand dollars, and I figured if I had nothing else to do, I might as well go to SF full-time and do my podcast, hoping something would fall into place.

My Airbnb for the summer turned out to be a fake listing, so I had to stay in a hostel with shared rooms for almost three weeks until I found a more permanent place, which was the Minerva building at 16 Turk Street in the Tenderloin — it was ancient, decrepit, had no amenities, and I shared a dorm-style room with one other guy. It was $950 a month. That was summer 2024.

When I got to SF, I had about a thousand Twitter followers. I posted some good tweets in the first couple weeks that doubled me to about 2,000, and I started meeting people in real life, partly through Manifold Markets’s Taco Tuesdays, hosted by Manifold. I got to know Stephen Grugett and Austin Chen and, to a lesser extent, James Grugett. I met a lot of Twitter people, tech people, rationalists, in real life. In May, a couple weeks after I arrived, I went to a Scott Alexander meetup at Lighthaven in Berkeley. It was my first time there. I fell in love with the place. There were so many people there I knew from the internet, and the venue itself is beautiful.

That weekend was Manifest. I had discounted student tickets. It was the greatest time of my life. It was incredible to be around all these people who lived and breathed the stuff I’d been reading and writing about on Twitter. By that point, I’d been on Twitter for almost two years and had been posting for about a year.

I should mention that I heavily credit Stevie Miller, above just about anyone, for helping me get into this. We’ve known each other since we were about eight. We went to the same elementary school in Florida for a couple of years. He moved to D.C. but kept visiting because his grandmother lived in Florida. He introduced me first to Neoreaction, then to Curtis Yarvin, then to the SF rationalists. I found LessWrong independently, but he showed me it was a whole movement — told me about Manifold Taco Tuesday, told me about Manifest. I owe an immense debt to Stevie.

During summer 2024, I applied for and got an Emergent Ventures grant from Tyler Cowen’s Mercatus Center. That’s what let me survive in SF the rest of the summer. I came back to school after that, constantly thinking about going back to SF.

Stylish Literature

A rarely remarked-upon corollary to the supposed death of reading would be the death of literary style — the absence of young writers more famous for being in the world than for writing about it, who cultivate a look for the jacket cover, the camera, and the cocktail hour. But reading is not dead, nor is literary style. Need we look further than George Monaghan?

Monaghan is the newly appointed Newsletters Editor at Britain’s The New Statesman, where he was formerly Junior Commissioning Editor. For Monaghan, there need not be a trade-off between pleasure and writing; the 27-year-old talks about literature not with brooding melancholy, but with a grin. He evades the depressed, self-imposed asceticism of the lonely writer toiling away in obscurity, all while remaining serious about literature.

George and I discuss London’s contemporary intellectual life and the ambitions of young and optimistic British writers in an age of literary pessimism.

Political Betrayal

The spectacle of online debate, of “owning the libs,” is now a rite of passage for the budding conservative commentator. Shabbos Kestenbaum, a 26-year-old Orthodox Jew, is the latest in this tradition of fast-talkers, a professional lineage that includes Charlie Kirk and Ben Shapiro. A quick Google search displays videos of Shabbos “debunking Anna [sic] Kasparian’s deranged conspiracies straight to her face,” and a photo of Shabbos and Sebastian Gorka (Trump official and dismantler of America’s counter-terrorism apparatus) smoking cigars on July 4th.

But before October 7th, Shabbos was a member of the Democratic Party, a Bernie Sanders supporter, and master’s student at Harvard Divinity School. A few months later, Shabbos had sued Harvard for antisemitism (in May of 2025, he agreed to a confidential settlement); his political star began to rise.

In 2024, Kestenbaum spoke at the Republican National Convention (“I am a proud first-generation American, I am a proud Orthodox Jew, and as of five months ago, I am the proud plaintiff suing Harvard University for its failure to combat antisemitism”) and endorsed President Trump; later, The New York Times profiled Kestenbaum as “The Jewish Student Who Took On Harvard.”

Now Shabbos works as commentator for PragerU, a publication and YouTube channel founded by Dennis Prager that “helps people of all ages think and live better while upholding Judeo-Christian values.” He lives in Los Angeles, where he makes podcasts and YouTube videos, and travels the country raising money for Zionist causes while warning of antisemitism’s corrosive spread.

What follows is Shabbos’s own articulation of his ideological journey.

New Right Whisperer

New Right Whisperer

In January of 2025, Mana Afsari uncovered the El Dorado of American politics: a new angle. Her essay, “Last Boys at the Beginning of History,” published in The Point, argued that the army of Trump-worshipping young men, members of the New Right, were not all just flippant misogynists. They were men, or boys, really, hungry for meaning in a political world that dismissed questions of purpose and greatness.

After spending time at both the National Conservatism conference and the liberal “Unpopulist” conference in D.C., Afsari found something missing in liberalism.

A year later, Afsari wrote a follow-up on dating, “Doomers in Love,” about those young people giving up on the possibility of a happy romantic life and their excuses for being single.

In these two essays, Mana Afsari has announced herself as a pre-eminent gen z intellectual and whisperer of the New Right.

One narrative that became especially dominant was the end of liberalism. Having worked at organizations that were classically liberal and defended civil liberties, I found that cultural renunciation of liberalism, whatever it means, was dominant everywhere except inside mainstream liberal institutions. If you’re our age, you take it for granted that liberalism has had problems, that the sort of civil discourse — driven, consensus-driven politics — have not been practiced for some time. But I was working at places like FIRE (Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression) right out of college. I was familiar enough with that world — with the people who organized the liberalism conferences — to know that they were not fully aware of the extent of the crisis. They (I mean the entire ecosystem, not any one specifically) were still putting on conferences, often for only elite people, and not really reaching out to young people and asking why they were so frustrated.

There are some sensitive, thoughtful liberal defenders — Mark Lilla is the apex here. Francis Fukuyama, in personal conversation and obviously with his original “End of History” essay, does a great job of really understanding what’s going on, and is open about what he doesn’t understand. But there’s still a resistance faction that completely misapprehends gen z’s political and digital rebellions as only a superficial, bigoted, reactionary, thoughtless trend.

What my first essay did — and what I still believe to be true — is that despite the fact that there absolutely is a portion of this reaction, on the right and left, that is reactionary, prejudicial, knee-jerk, there are deeper moral aspirations beneath all of it. A lot of these people have a hard time wrapping their head around how hard it must be to be a young person facing a culture in which you feel you have no role. Mark Lilla, in his excellent new book of essays Ignorance and Bliss, which I think is very underrated, has a paragraph where he says young people today awake every morning in a new Potemkin village. Unlike Odysseus, life is not about firmly planting your feet and figuring out where you ought to be. It’s waking up every morning in a completely new world.

Many of us could choose to disconnect from the internet that perpetuates this world of disconnect and alienation, but the reality remains that everything feels much more anarchic and fluid than that. I don’t even think it’s liberalism that is the problem — “liberalism,” to [its young critics], is just a shorthand for the previous era’s pretenses. Those commitments are going to be collateral damage if this instability continues.

Overall, I do think gen z has an inertia problem, a paralysis problem, and a fear problem. I think a lot of these illegible and dizzying trends and phenomena — looksmaxxing, groypers, the identity obsession on parts of the left that ultimately amounts to role-playing — are crises of self-fashioning that would be largely unintelligible to someone like Mark Lilla, who I guess will become a metaphor in this entire conversation. If you’re a boomer, you grew up against a bunch of residual “shoulds” in a more morally uniform culture, and it’s satisfying to chart your own course. Whereas now, we have nothing. There is no good and evil, so we can’t really go “beyond good and evil” as a generation. There’s nothing to rebel against, and so there’s a paralysis, a crisis of self-trust, an inability to make our own decisions. Seeking our own self-made limitations of various kinds allows us the form we need in a fluid world.

You’re a great example, Owen, of someone who goes back into the tradition, engages with it on its own terms, actually has an interior experience with it, and fashions something new into the culture. That’s a fantastic template for gen z. It’s what every successful generation has done. And it only requires 10 to 20 thoughtful people in a country like ours to actually push the culture forward and keep something of that sacred spring alive for the next generation.
